summary: For ages 7–9: the ocean floor is not a flat sandy bottom but a hidden landscape of mountains, mid-ocean ridges, flat abyssal plains, tall seamounts and deep trenches — resembling kinds of features also found on dry land. The memorable scale anchor is that the Mariana Trench's Challenger Deep (~10,935 m per NOAA) is deeper than Mount Everest (8,848 m) is tall, so Everest dropped into the trench would still have its summit roughly 2 km underwater. Learners should finish able to state the seafloor has varied terrain, name the Mariana Trench as the deepest point, and use the Everest comparison to convey how deep that is.
misconceptions: 'The ocean floor is a flat, sandy bottom' — missing its mountains, ridges and trenches.
'The ocean is the same depth everywhere' — not knowing depth varies enormously.
'Mount Everest is the biggest vertical feature on Earth' — the Mariana Trench is deeper than Everest is tall.
Confusing the deep TRENCH (a narrow gash) with the ocean being uniformly that deep everywhere.
'Nothing could be under that much water' — not yet knowing life exists even in the deepest trenches (sets up deep-sea topics).

activities.title: Tap across a to-scale seafloor profile
steps: Before seeing the profile, predict aloud what the bare seabed would look like if all the water drained away — flat and smooth, or varied? Then study a wide to-scale cross-section running from the shore outward across an ocean basin: continental shelf → slope → abyssal plain with seamounts → mid-ocean ridge → abyssal plain → a deep trench near the far edge, beside an island arc.
Tap or point to each feature in turn (ridge, seamount, abyssal plain, trench) and say its name and one fact about it.
Check your earlier prediction against the profile: is the bare seabed flat and smooth, or varied? Say what surprised you.
Compare each undersea feature to a land feature it resembles (undersea mountain range, deep valley) and state that the seafloor has similar kinds of features to dry land, just hidden underwater.
activities.insight: The ocean floor has varied terrain — mountains, ridges, plains and deep trenches — not a uniform flat sandy bottom, and these resemble landforms found on land.

activities.title: Drop Everest into the trench
steps: Look at a vertical depth ruler marked in metres, with the sunlit surface zone at top and Challenger Deep at the bottom.
Place (or trigger a 'drop Everest in' control that places) Mount Everest upright, with its base on the floor of Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, beside the ruler.
Read where Everest's summit stops and state that it is still roughly 2 km below the surface — the mountain is fully drowned.
Answer: which is greater, Everest's height (8,848 m) or the trench's depth (~10,935 m)? Then say the deepest point of the ocean is deeper than the highest mountain is tall.
Name the Mariana Trench (Challenger Deep) as the deepest point on Earth.
activities.insight: Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench (~10,935 m) is deeper than Mount Everest (8,848 m) is tall, so Everest would still sit about 2 km underwater — a memorable way to grasp how deep the ocean's deepest point is.

activities.title: Fly or dive to the deepest point (enrichment)
steps: Travel along the seafloor in a flythrough or a descending submersible: skim an underwater mountain range, cross the flat abyssal plain, then plunge into the Mariana Trench.
Watch a live depth readout and call out when it passes 8,848 m — the 'Everest height' milestone — on the way down to ~10,935 m at the trench floor.
Describe aloud how the relief and depth change along the journey, and how far past the Everest milestone the descent continues.
activities.insight: Seafloor terrain is genuinely three-dimensional; travelling over ridges and down into the trench can convey relief and the depth of the descent, reinforcing the varied-terrain and scale ideas.

activities.title: Check and explain the seafloor
steps: Answer: is the seafloor flat, or does it have varied terrain? Give at least one feature to support your answer.
Name the deepest point on Earth (the Mariana Trench / Challenger Deep).
Compare: which is greater, Mount Everest's height or the Mariana Trench's depth?

Explain WHY the seabed is shaped this way — its mountains, ridges and trenches are made and moved by the same Earth forces (moving crust, volcanoes) that build mountains and volcanoes on land. Water does not level the whole floor flat, though mud slowly settling on the bottom does help make the abyssal plains flat.
Respond to the drained-ocean prompt: 'A child says the bare seabed would be flat and smooth like a giant bathtub, maybe sloping a bit. Do you agree? What would we actually walk over, and why?'
activities.insight: Learners can state the seafloor has varied terrain, name the Mariana Trench as the deepest point, use the Everest comparison, and begin to explain the relief as the result of Earth's crustal and volcanic processes rather than water levelling.

checkQuestion: Imagine we drained all the water out of the ocean and could walk across the bare seabed. A child says 'it would be flat and smooth, like the bottom of a giant bathtub, maybe sloping down a bit'. Do you think that's what we'd find — and if not, what would we walk over, and why is it shaped that way?
checkAnswer: The ocean floor is not flat — it has the biggest mountains, deepest valleys and longest ranges on Earth: gently sloping continental shelves near land, vast flat plains, huge undersea mountain chains (mid-ocean ridges), tall volcanic seamounts, and deep narrow trenches. The Mariana Trench is deeper than Mount Everest is tall. It's shaped this way because the seabed is made and moved by the same forces that build mountains and volcanoes on land, not by water settling flat.
